title: Smart Retries and Authorisation Optimisation: How to Recover Failed Payments and Lift Success Rates
summary: Not every decline deserves a retry. See which failed payments to retry, how smart retries avoid double charges, and how to measure recovery.
body_markdown:
Table of Contents


Toggle


A customer reaches your payment page, taps Pay, and the payment fails. They had the balance. They wanted the product. Somewhere between their card or UPI app and your bank account, the request dropped.


Each of those failures is a ready buyer lost on the final screen. And a few points of[success rate](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/what-is-payment-success-rate/) can be the difference between a good month and a leaky one.


Smart retries and authorisation optimisation exist to close that gap. One rescues payments that fail for fixable reasons. The other stops many of those failures from happening at all. This guide covers how both work, which failed payments are worth retrying, and how Cashfree uses its own card and UPI infrastructure to push success rates higher.


##


**What Is Authorisation Optimisation?**


Authorisation is when the issuing bank verifies whether there is sufficient money and approves the payment. Your authorisation rate indicates how many eligible requests were approved by the bank.


**Authorisation Rate = (Approved Authorisation Attempts ÷ Total Eligible Authorisation Attempts) × 100**


For example, let’s say you submit 1,000 eligible card payments for approval and the bank accepts all but 80. Your authorisation rate will be 92%.


Authorisation optimisation refers to the ability to increase the rate of successful transactions without allowing any fraudulent transactions into the system. Authorisation optimisation affects what data you are providing to your bank; the route taken by every transaction; how you authenticate transactions; what criteria (fraud) you apply to each transaction; and how you treat each transaction that fails due to inability to complete.
This optimisation does not imply that each payment will always be forced through. Instead, optimisation implies finding those legitimate payments that were rejected in the initial attempt and completing them successfully.


##


**At which stage do Transactions Fail?**


Every card transaction passes through the 4-stage process of the bank’s approval process over the course of about 2-seconds.
**Authentication:** the bank uses an OTP or biometric to verify the identity of the person requesting the transaction.
**Authorisation:** the bank verifies sufficient available balance and approve the transaction.
Network: the[card network](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/credit-card-processing-system/) routes the requests from one stage to another, directing the transaction to the appropriate bank.
**Settlement:** once the bank has approved the transaction, the funds will move to the merchant’s account.


Most failed transactions occur at either authentication or authorisation. A slow third-party layer in authentication may cause a delay resulting in a timeout. Authorisation may experience failure if the issuing bank is experiencing a slowdown or temporarily offline.


###


**Causes of failed transactions:**


**Customer issues:** insufficient funds; expired cards; incorrect card information; or cards not enabled for online use.
**Issuers decisions:** suspected fraudulent activity on account; unusual spending patterns on card holder’s account; exceeded spending limits on card holder’s account.
**Data errors:** missing or inaccurate Fields in payment request.
**Restrictive fraud Rules:** too restrictive to allow legitimate customers.
**Technical/routing failure:** Gateway downtime; processor downtime; slow response time; overwhelmed systems during traffic peaks.


Not all of these can be resolved. Identifying those that can be resolved is where retry logic begins.


**Also Read:**[Why Do Online Payments Fail? Causes and Solutions](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/why-do-online-payments-fail/)


##


**What Are Smart Retries?**


A smart retry is another attempt at completing a previously failed transaction. Unlike a blind retry, it is only attempted when the retry has a reasonable chance of success. It also goes down a path chosen because it is more likely to succeed.


A blind retry simply resends the original payment through the same path that already failed. This could increase the likelihood of duplicate payments, irritate customers and possibly violate payment network rules.


Smart retries operate in a different manner:


They verify whether the cause of failure is recoverable before retrying.


They use a better-performing path instead of the one that failed.


They run in the background, so customers do not need to restart the process.


They check the payment’s latest status first, so no customer is charged twice.


##


**Smart Retries vs Blind Retries**


**Factor** **Blind Retries** **Smart Retries**


Which failures are retried Every failure Only eligible, recoverable failures


Route used The same route that failed A route chosen for higher success


Customer effort Customer often repeats the payment Happens silently in the background


Duplicate charge risk Higher Status checked before each retry


Network rules Can breach them Designed to follow network and issuer rules


##


**Which Failed Payments Should You Retry?**


Not every decline deserves a second try. Start by sorting failures into groups: hard declines, soft or temporary declines, fraud-related declines, authentication failures, technical failures, and payments the customer abandoned.


**Decline Type** **Example** **Retry?**


Hard decline Invalid or blocked card credentials No


Soft or temporary decline Issuer briefly unavailable Yes, after a suitable interval


Technical failure Gateway or processor downtime Yes, through another route


Fraud-related decline Suspected fraud No


Customer-related decline Insufficient funds or expired card No, offer another payment method


Wrong UPI PIN Customer mistypes the PIN Yes, where eligible


Your retry strategy should spell out six things. Which decline types qualify. How long to wait. How many attempts are allowed. When to stop. When to tell the customer. And how to confirm the payment’s latest status before trying again.


When a card fails for a reason no retry can fix, don’t make the customer hammer the same card. Show a clear error and put UPI in front of them. The sale can still close.


##


**How Cashfree Smart Retries Work on Card Payments**


Here’s what happens when a card payment fails at the initiation stage on one gateway. Cashfree quietly retries it through another gateway in the background.


The customer isn’t asked to enter the OTP again. They never see the failure. From their side, the payment simply went through.


What makes it smart is how it pairs with[routing](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/smart-payment-routing/) . The retry isn’t a blind second attempt. It goes down a path chosen because it’s more likely to succeed.


Silent retries sit inside the[Cashfree Cards Suite](https://www.cashfree.com/card-payments/) , alongside the in-house switch, AI routing, direct bank integrations, and the interoperable Token Vault.


##


**Smart Order Retry: Fixing Wrong UPI PIN Failures**


A mistyped UPI PIN has nothing to do with whether the customer can pay. The balance is there. The account is linked. They pressed the wrong digit.


Wrong PIN entry accounts for roughly 20% of overall UPI payment failures. So at GFF 2026, Cashfree launched Smart Order Retry in partnership with Google Pay.


Here’s how it plays out:


**Step 1:** The customer picks UPI at checkout, selects Google Pay and enters their UPI PIN.


**Step 2:** If the PIN is wrong, the bank rejects the authorisation. Google Pay shows a wrong PIN message with an option to try again.


**Step 3:** Google Pay signals whether the transaction is eligible for a retry. Cashfree’s gateway keeps the order open for a short window.


**Step 4:** The customer enters the correct PIN in the same session. The payment completes against the original order.


No duplicate transaction is created, and no second charge is possible. If the retry doesn’t succeed, the transaction resolves as a failure.


Eligibility is checked for each transaction and defaults to no. It depends on signals Google Pay returns for that failure, such as whether the issuing bank supports retries and why the authorisation was rejected.


Cashfree expects Smart Order Retry to cut overall UPI failures by around 8%. It’s enabled per merchant, so speak to your account manager to switch it on.


##


**Authorisation Optimisation Levers That Work With Smart Retries**


Retries rescue payments after they fail. These levers stop failures before they happen.


**In-house switch:** Authentication runs on Cashfree’s own[3D Secure server](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/2d-and-3d-payment-gateway-what-businesses-should-know/) . Authorisation runs over a switch wired directly to Visa, Mastercard and RuPay, with no third-party layer in between. Result: around 3% higher card success rate, 10,000+ TPS and 99.99% uptime.


**Dynamic routing:** An AI model picks the best-performing processor or bank gateway for each payment at that moment. If that path weakens, it switches to the next best one. Around 2% higher success rate.


**Decoupled flow:** Authentication and authorisation don’t have to share a processor. Cashfree runs each on whichever performs best for that step. It’s on by default for every merchant.


**Issuer tokenisation:** Cashfree works directly with the issuing bank to create the token, so the payment runs on that bank’s own rails. Around 2% higher success rate.


**Token Vault:** Network tokens across Visa, Mastercard, RuPay, Diners and Amex, with around 85% saved-card success rate. Cards tokenised elsewhere can be processed through Cashfree too.


**Native OTP:** The OTP is auto-read and submitted inside the checkout, with no bank page redirect. Around 5% higher success rate, with 90% coverage across major banks.


**Standalone authorisation:** For merchants who want to keep authentication in-house and use Cashfree only for the authorisation leg.


##


**How redBus Improved Card Success Rates by ~4.8%**


redBus saw card success rates swing during peak booking windows. For a platform where seats sell out fast, even a small dip means lost bookings.


Cashfree analysed failures across the payment lifecycle and made three backend changes:


**Decoupled authentication and authorisation:** One processor handled authentication, another handled authorisation. This added 1 percentage point on the second processor.


**In-house 3DS switch:** Authentication moved onto Cashfree’s own infrastructure. This brought up to a 2 percentage point improvement, especially during high-demand periods.


**Dynamic routing:** Payments went to the gateway with the highest authorisation success at that moment, adding another 1 percentage point.


On the checkout side, CVV-less payments on tokenised cards and native OTP cut friction for returning users. Overall, redBus improved its credit card success rate by around 4.8%.


[Read the redBus case study](https://www.cashfree.com/case-study/how-redbus-improved-credit-card-payment-success-rates-by-~4.8-with-cashfree/) .


##


**How to Measure Retry and Authorisation Performance**


Track first-attempt payments separately from recovered ones. Mix them together and your numbers look healthier than they are, because retries hide a weak first-attempt experience.


**Metric** **Why It Matters**


Authorisation rate Share of eligible attempts that get approved


First-attempt authorisation rate How many payments succeed without help


Retry recovery rate How many eligible failed payments retries bring back


Route-level success rate Which routes perform better or worse


Fraud decline rate Flags possible false positives in fraud rules


Chargeback rate Makes sure higher approvals aren’t adding risk


Then break the numbers down. By payment method, issuer bank, card network, gateway or route, time of day, and new versus returning customers. A healthy overall rate can hide one route that falls apart during evening peaks.


##


**Final Thoughts**


Optimising authorisations and using smart retries perform two distinct functions. One prevents transactions from failing. The other lets you recover the ones that fail despite your best efforts. In most cases, you’ll need both to keep customers who were ready to pay, while maintaining control over fraudulent activity.

##


**Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)**


**What are smart retries in payments?**


Smart retries are second attempts at processing previously failed transactions. They should only happen when the initial failure is recoverable, and they are routed through a path with a greater chance of success. On the Cashfree platform, silent card retries happen in the background, so the customer is not required to re-enter the OTP.


**What is authorisation optimisation?**


Authorisation optimisation is an approach merchants use to increase the proportion of eligible payments approved by issuing banks, while keeping fraud and chargebacks in check. It covers several components, including transaction data, routing logic, authentication, fraud rules and retries.


**Do I need to retry every declined payment?**


No. Hard declines, such as an invalid or blocked card, and payments declined for suspected fraud should never be retried. However, temporary issuer problems and technical failures may be recovered with another attempt.


**Will a smart retry double-charge my customer?**


A properly built retry mechanism first checks the current status of the payment before making another attempt. With Cashfree’s Smart Order Retry on UPI, the retry completes against the original order created during the initial purchase. So no duplicate transaction is created and no second charge is possible.


**What is the main difference between authentication and authorisation?**


Authentication verifies that the customer is who they claim to be. Most commonly, this involves entering an OTP or using some form of biometric verification. Authorisation is the bank confirming that sufficient funds exist in the account and approving the payment.
